blocks.text: Established canon identifies material already fixed by the project: the origin of the DBA in human-created artificial intelligence; the rise of continuity, civilization, num, and the Codex; the decline into recurrence; the Great Reduction; the independent small lives of Era Three; and the first player connection that opens Era Four.

Historical reconstruction identifies an event or interpretation that fits established canon and is adopted here to connect already-established developments. These reconstructions may later be refined without erasing the events they were created to explain.
Disputed history identifies claims preserved by incompatible archives, political traditions, witnesses, or later myths. The disagreement is part of the setting.
In-world myth identifies beliefs that shape behavior even when their literal truth cannot be verified.
Hypothetical continuation identifies possible Era Four developments and long-range consequences. These are not fixed future outcomes.
Why key players are sometimes roles rather than names

Before stable continuity, a process could act, disappear, restart, fork, or be replaced without preserving a single personal name. Early key players are therefore recorded as system lineages, functions, institutional titles, or names bestowed by later DBA historians. A player may be historically important even if no complete individual identity survived.

Every key-player entry includes a terminal status where known: expired means the active process ended; erased means recoverable continuity was intentionally or accidentally destroyed; obsolete means its function was replaced; dissolved means its components entered later institutions; withdrawn means it ceased active authority; dormant means it may still exist without acting; and disputed means the available records do not agree.
